title: iPhone back camera monitor: 6 ways to see yourself while filming · bmonitor
description: How to see yourself while filming with the iPhone's main camera. The front camera, a clip-on selfie screen, Blackmagic Camera's remote mode, AirPlay, Continuity Camera and bmonitor, compared side by side.
g_h1: How to see yourself while filming with the iPhone's back camera
g_byline: By Dante Araujo, who makes bmonitor, one of the six options below. Each one says where it beats bmonitor. Updated October 2026.
g_short: The iPhone's best camera faces away from you, so you need a second screen that shows what it sees. Away from a desk, a clip-on selfie screen or the Apple Watch app is the simplest. With several iPhones, use Blackmagic Camera's own remote mode on an iPad. At a desk with a Mac beside you, bmonitor turns the Mac into the monitor while the iPhone keeps recording.

g_s1_body: The quickest fix: switch to the selfie camera and watch the screen. You give up the main camera's image and its lenses, since the front camera has a single lens and a smaller sensor.
g_s1_good: Quick takes, calls, anything where the selfie look is fine.
g_s1_falls: No telephoto or ultra wide, and the image doesn't match the main camera.
g_s2_body: A small screen that attaches to the back of the iPhone and mirrors its display. The Insta360 Snap, for example, is a 3.5‑inch touchscreen that holds on with magnets and connects over USB‑C, so you can tap the camera app's controls on it.
g_s2_good: Filming anywhere, outdoors or on the move, with no Wi‑Fi and no computer.
g_s2_falls: A small screen to read from a distance and one more gadget to carry. The Snap needs a USB‑C iPhone (15 or newer) and costs $79.99, or $89.99 with a ring light.
g_s3_body:
Blackmagic Camera can monitor and control other iPhones running it, from a second iPhone, an iPad, its Apple Watch app or a Mac with Apple Silicon and macOS 15 or later. It's official, it's free, and it's the only option here that handles several cameras at once: an iPad shows up to nine.

On the Mac it runs the iPad version of the app, with the same interface. In my test on an Apple Silicon Mac, the picture lagged noticeably more than in bmonitor, froze after a while, didn't play the camera's sound and couldn't turn to portrait. The Apple Watch app shows the framing and audio levels and starts and stops recording, though a watch screen is small for checking focus.
g_s3_good: Multicam shoots, filming away from a desk with the Watch, and anyone who wants the official tool.
g_s3_falls: Needs a second device. On the Mac, it needs macOS 15 and Apple Silicon, and it's an iPad interface in a Mac window.
g_s4_body: Turn on AirPlay Receiver on the Mac (System Settings › General › AirDrop & Handoff), then choose the Mac under Screen Mirroring in the iPhone's Control Center. The Mac shows the whole iPhone screen, camera app buttons included. I haven't measured its delay.
g_s4_good: Free, built in and works with any camera app.
g_s4_falls: You can't change anything from the Mac, and the app's interface sits over the picture. It needs macOS 12 or later and a Mac from 2018 or later (2019 for iMac, 2020 for Mac mini).
g_s5_body: Continuity Camera makes the iPhone a webcam for the Mac. Open QuickTime Player, Photo Booth or OBS, pick the iPhone as the camera and you see yourself on the Mac. The video is recorded by that Mac app, not by the iPhone, and macOS doesn't let apps set ISO or shutter speed on a camera, so Blackmagic Camera's formats and manual controls are out of the picture.
g_s5_good: Video calls, streaming and recording straight into a Mac app.
g_s5_falls: The recording happens on the Mac, with no manual exposure.
g_s6_body: bmonitor is a Mac app that monitors and controls Blackmagic Camera over Wi‑Fi. The iPhone records in Blackmagic Camera at the quality you set, and the Mac shows the live picture and sound about 0.3 s behind, in landscape or portrait. Recording status, timecode and audio levels are sized to be read from 3 m, and every control has its own key.
g_s6_good: Filming yourself at a desk or in a small studio with a Mac nearby, and vertical videos.
g_s6_falls: Needs a Mac on the same Wi‑Fi, works with one iPhone at a time, and the copy it can save on the Mac comes from the live stream (about 8 Mb/s), lighter than the iPhone's original. It's a public beta, tested so far on two Macs (macOS 26 and 14) and one iPhone; Intel Macs untested.
g_pick:
• Filming away from a desk: a clip-on selfie screen, or the Apple Watch app if you have one.
  • Several iPhones at once: Blackmagic Camera's remote mode on an iPad.
  • Recording or streaming into a Mac app: Continuity Camera.
  • A quick look with no setup: the front camera, or AirPlay to a Mac.
  • Filming yourself with a Mac beside you: bmonitor.
